articles.author: MaxHuo
articles.description:
When people first learn about object storage, replication sounds like the obvious answer.
Need durability?
Keep three copies.
Need higher availability?
Keep more copies.
Simple.
For years, that's exactly what many storage systems did.
Then storage clusters became enormous.
Imagine storing:
10 PB

of data.
With three-way replication, you don't actually need 10 PB of storage.
You need:
30 PB

Suddenly, durability isn't just a technical problem.
It's a financial one.
At cloud scale, every extra copy costs millions of dollars in disks, racks, power, cooling, and networking.
Storage engineers started asking a different question.
Can we protect data without storing complete copies?
That question led to one of the biggest architectural shifts in modern object storage.
Suppose you upload:
vacation…
articles.title: Why Modern Object Storage Doesn't Just Keep Three Copies

articles.author: TheMMR
articles.description:
At first when I started using AI, it was like talking to a genius kid. It was brilliant but couldn't get the grasp of what you are saying. later on it grew and grew to the point which now we cannot imagine our lives without using it anymore.
When I was working on a project for lexoya.com, at first i didn't trust AI, but later on i realized that it has many capabilities and if I don't use it, i won't be able to keep up with the other guys that are using it without any break. 
I had the idea that i would tell the AI to go do this and Bam! it would get it done, but now i understand that we should use AI as a Junior and as someone who needs guidance to do the stuff. Of course you can use AI for difficult and complex subject but you can get the most of it when you exactly know what you want and you just tell the AI to implement it.
I like how the AI is changing our lives and how we are learning how to talk and treat the AIs.
I wish we could do the same and would actually try to learn how to talk and communicate. :)
articles.title: How my view of AI is changing

articles.author: Mohit Patel
articles.description:
One afternoon, I opened my browser and looked at the bookmarks bar.
There were 47 bookmarks.
Most of them had been sitting there for years.
Articles I planned to read.
Courses I promised myself I'd finish.
Documentation I'd "need someday."
Tools I'd forgotten existed.
It looked organized.
But it wasn't useful.
So I deleted almost all of them.
Surprisingly...
I haven't missed a single one.
Saving something feels productive.
Bookmarking an article feels like learning.
Saving a course feels like making progress.
Adding another YouTube video to "Watch Later" feels responsible.
But nothing actually changes.
Knowledge isn't collected.
It's applied.
Most of us don't just hoard physical things.
We hoard digital ones too.
Bookmarks
PDFs
Screenshots
Browser tabs
Notes
Courses
GitHub repositories
We …
articles.title: I Deleted 47 Browser Bookmarks and Didn't Regret It

articles.author: Nazar Boyko
articles.description:
Typosquatting bets on your typo. Slopsquatting bets on your AI assistant. When a model invents a package that doesn't exist, an attacker registers the name and waits for install to run. Here's the kill chain, why your usual defenses miss it, and what actually stops it across npm, Composer, and pip.
Imagine a coding assistant just told you to run this:
pip install requests-oauth2-helper

It looks right. You asked for a clean way to attach OAuth2 tokens to your requests calls, and the name reads exactly like a package that would do that. The casing is idiomatic, the hyphenation matches the ecosystem, it sounds like fifty other real PyPI helpers. So you run it. Tests pass. You move on.
The problem is that requests-oauth2-helper never existed when the model learned to suggest it. The model mad…
articles.title: Slopsquatting: The Supply Chain Attack That Weaponizes AI Hallucinations

By Hudson Atwell, GBTI Network Member. Originally published on gbti.network.
Claude Code loads any markdown file at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md as a reusable slash command (a "skill"). This one gives your agent a /sow command for managing Scopes of Work: local, lane-based planning documents that move kanban-style from queue to completed, living beside your code but outside version control.
It exists because agent-driven projects accumulate work items faster than anyone can track them in their head. A SOW gives every work item one canonical markdown file with a status banner, phases, and open questions; the lanes give the whole project a glanceable board; and the authoring rules keep the agent from duplicating items or writing plans detached from the real code.
